With Valeri Ponzo. After leaving Fred W. Coyle Freedom Park in Naples, we came here. The boardwalk was a favored stop, but it has been closed for three years (?) as it was rebuilt and rerouted east. There is a now a center here, from which the new boardwalk begins. Owing it being Valentine's Day weekend, the park fee ($3 per person) is waived and the park is free. The new trail joins with the former trail north of the Miccosukee village. The total length of the boardwalk and trail is 1 mile. It took us almost 2.4 hours to get to the end, but a bit more than an hour back; such is the pace we were moving heading out. We were the last to leave, and the park ranger locked the gate behind us. The weather at the start was partly cloudy, 79 degrees ("feels like" 81), and with SW winds at 8 MPH. We arrived at 1400 and left at 1813.

With Don Fraser; the annual DeLuca Preserve bioblitz, with more than 100 participants. The weather at the start was partly sunny, foggy (which burned off quickly afterward), 69 degrees ("feels like" 69), and a light breeze. The weather at our departure was sunny, low 80s, with a light breeze. 

I left Spring Hill at 0430 and joined Don at Clearwater at 0535. We arrived at the preserve at 0820 and immediately went to the moth array at the sign-in spot/campground. Even at 0830, the sheet was great! (I can only wonder what it was like last night -- or what it will be like tonight!). Afterward, we checked a moth trap not too far away, and this too held some goodies.

Don and I were our own party. Due to the severe, prolonged drought, there were "no" flowers blooming, and we saw very few butterflies (all of them small species) and no moths nectaring. The few swallowtails were saw were in sustained flight and I got no photographs of any of them. Most wetlands were dry; we saw standing water in only a few drainage ditches. Dragonflies were scarce, except that we saw several Halloween Pennants at a patch of not-yet-blooming Nuttall's Thistles. "Bugs" were similarly scarce or absent, with no beetles, velvet ants, robber flies, and wasps seen at all, and just a few bees seen. Flies were restricted to a few Condylostylus at the thistle patch. Birds were mostly limited to Tree Swallows, Pine Warblers, American Crows, and two Eastern Phoebes on barbed-wire fencing near (dead) orchards.

I apologize in advance for the poor quality of some of today's photographs. Normally, I delete photographs such as these, but since this was part of a bioblitz, I have included them.

I gathered 285 records: 41 records of moths and other insects at the moth arrays, and 244 records elsewhere, mostly of plants in flatwoods or dry prairies.

We left shortly after 1332.

A: This is a native species to the southeastern U.S and is very common in Georgia.

B: Muscadine vine is not invasive. While it can spread and climb it doesn't typically out compete or harm native plant communities.

C: Muscadines provide a excellent value for wildlife species. The grapes are eaten by deer, opossums, raccoons, songbirds, and turkeys. The vine structure also offers cover and escape habitat, and its leaves may be browsed by the deer. It is especially valuable as a seasonal soft mast source.

D: This plant is highly desirable in the understory and a long the woodlines. It should be left and even encouraged, especially in wildlife management areas. Some control may be needed if it becomes overly dense in timber stands but for the most part they are considered beneficial.

A solo visit because I needed to get out. This morning was cool and overcast with occasional light rain; I waited until mid-afternoon to go out. The weather at the start was sunny, 81 degrees ("feels like" 84), with ENE winds at 12 MPH.

1535-1557: Rattlesnake Road thistle pond east to the road to the north. On foot. Not much was happening. I flushed a metalmark but all my photographs of it were hideously unfocused and were discarded.

1606-1754: Rattlesnake Camp Road, west end, the southern tram. On foot. I was surprised by many patches of standing water; it must been raining here. Nor was I prepared for all the mosquitoes, but I soldiered on. There must have been more than a hundred satyrs along the tram; literally, one-three would flush every 10-12 feet for a mile. I didn't realize at the time that most were Little Satyrs! I don't remember seeing them along this tram before (but I must have?). Otherwise, spring renewal and greening are well underway. I found a "blooming" Florida Jack-in-the-Pulpit. :)

A solo visit to check out blooming plants and the "bugs" that feed on them. The weather at my arrival (1158) was sunny, 75 degrees ("feels like" 75), with WNW winds at 7 MPH. The weather at the end (1536) was sunny, 77 degrees ("feels like" 77), with W winds at 10 MPH. I saw Dale Goebels and Nicky Armstrong along Rattlesnake Camp Road shortly at my arrival; they were leaving after arriving at 0800. In checking the Chassahowitzka WEA iNat project, I noticed that I have 975 species -- by no means all Research Graded! I'll try to hit 1,000 species in the next few visits. I visited two areas today as follows:

1205-1238: the forested wetland along Rattlesnake Camp Road just east of Scrub Island Road/3 Bridge Road. There were a number of Bristle Thistles in bloom here, with one Clouded Skipper and several swallowtails feeding on them.

1245-1438: the logging tram that heads westish from the turnaround at the end of Scrub Island Road. I walked farther along the tram than I have before. As seen during my most recent visit (14 Mar 2026), satyrs were common and almost all photographed with Little Wood Satyrs.

Afterward, I drove Rattlesnake Camp Road east to Gopher Road, then northwest to Thunder's Crossing Road, north to Indigo Lane, and north on North Road nearly to its end. I was looking for flowers, and other than two Bristle Thistles along Thunder's Crossing Road, I found none. I left at 1536.

A solo, spur-of-the-moment trip; a successful chase of the female Common Merganser (incredibly, my third in Pasco County [3 Apr 2009, 28 Dec 2016, and 30 Mar 2026], and my fourth in Florida, following a chase of one in Volusia County [17 Jan 2015]. Nathan Langwald apparently was first to discover this female a few days ago. Christine Rowland photographed it noonish today, and spread the word. Even though I was in need of a nap, I headed out almost immediately. So quickly that I did not replace my flash card from yesterday's birding excursion to SunWest Park. Neither John Swenfurth, Eric Plage, nor somebody whom I did not know, had an extra flash drive. Eventually, after Eric left, I drove to a nearby Walgreen's to buy a 32 GB flash card. I was very angry at myself for not having a spare flash card in my camera bag. (That's where the spares are supposed to be kept until an emergency!). I returned to the to the kayak launch to nobody else there. A kayaker joyously showed me a video he took of the merganser "less than five minutes ago" just off the launch. (The spot where the merganser had been seen previously). Fortunately, within two minutes, the merganser swam south to north past that spot, and then north to south one minute later. John and the other guy re-arrived at the kayak launch -- they had seen the merganser swim past them further down river. Afterward, I spent maybe 45 minutes looking for the merganser and photographing various plants for iNaturalist. I arrived at 1719, left at 1739 to buy a flash drive, then returned to Grey Preserve at 1804. I left at 1946 and headed home, arriving at 2009 while it was still light.

With Don Fraser; my first visit this year -- my, how times have changed! A visit to check on the Sparkleberry bushes. Many are in full bloom, some will be in full bloom in the next week or so, and we found at least two that are finishing flowering! We found one Fulvous Hairstreak and about eight Great Purple Hairstreaks. Nearly all other butterflies were scarce, although we saw several Common Buckeyes. I was surprised to see that the mowers have gone all around the property with the green barn, and presumably have mowed all the way to Aripeka Road. Not since 2015 have the mowers gone all around the property with the green barn. A large grass that grows commonly in clumps along the trail to the barn (I have never gotten a record RGed) must be an exotic, as somebody from Pasco County or SWFWMD has blitzed the hell of out most clumps. Several clumps are coming back, but the trail looks different now that the grass has been blitzed. We skipped the "back 40" acreage entirely to concentrate on the Sparkleberry bushes. We arrived at 0830 and left at 1210. The weather at the start was sunny, 69 degrees ("feels like" 69), with ESE winds at 7 MPH. The weather at the end was sunny, 80 degrees ("feels like" 82), with ESE winds at 9 MPH. We headed to Denny's for lunch.

With Don Fraser and maybe 35 others; an unsuccessful search for the Red-faced Warbler -- only the second record east of the Mississippi River (the other was in Georgia) -- found by a Texas woman on Friday and not reported on Saturday nearly until the park closed. So this was the first real day that birders could search for the warbler. The weather at the start was mostly sunny, 72 degrees (:feels like" 72), and with SSE winds at 9 MPH. It had rained heavily last night and maybe early this morning, The park opened at 0800 but we arrived (first!) at 0745 and waited for the office to open. A miscommunication led us all to search the wrong spot (it was RV Site 3, not Campsite #3), which most of us did not know about until after 1000. Don and I left at 1115 and headed to nearby Goethe State Forest for my first lifer butterfly (Crossline Skipper) in more than a year. Nobody saw the warbler today or yesterday.

This was a very neat (private) park that is popular with SCUBA divers and swimmers. In some ways, it is better maintained than a state park, which would allow yappy little dogs (and big dogs too) to enter the park and be a nuisance to almost everybody. Here, animals are prohibited. For the first time ever, we conducted this count in "developed" eastern Pasco County rather than in Green Swamp Wildlife and Environmental Area (mainly in Polk County) or in Colt Creek State Park in Polk  County. With Fran Meyerson; iNatting Citrus and Levy counties. Fran drove up in the morning, arriving about 1030, and we were quickly on our way, Our itinerary today was as follows:

1143-1338: Withlacoochee Bay Trail, Citrus County -- A "quick" stop to see if any Juniper Hairstreaks were on the Oakleaf Fleabane flowers. There were few flowers and no hairstreaks. The raised observation platform on the Gulf of Mexico was fairly seriously tilted to one side, presumably from one of the 2024 hurricanes, and was blocked off. Catchfly Prairie Gentian was blooming commonly. The weather at the start was sunny, 91 degrees ("feels like" 103), with WNW winds at 11 MPH.

1458-1748: Goethe State Forest, Cow Creek Road -- We arrived right after a shower drenched everything, and elected to drive to the Big Cypress Boardwalk. Fran photographed a Gemmed Satyr from the boardwalk! As soon as we got to "the" cypress, a lightning bolt hit within a few hundred feet. We retreated to Fran's SUV, where we enjoyed her homemade French Onion Soup. After 20 minutes, we ventured back out, heading east of Cow Creek Road along a recently clearcut area, where we stayed for two hours. Finally, we stopped twice along Cow Creek Road, but the few remaining blooming Nuttall's Thistles were skipperless. The weather at the start was overcast (sprinkling), 81 degrees ("feels like" 89), with W winds at 10 MPH.

1808-1948: SE 147th Place in Levy County -- A famous location for emperors and Goatweed Leafwings. We found four Hackberry Emperors and one Goatweed Leafwing, both lifers for Fran.

1949-2014: Cedars of Lebanon Cemetery at the east end of SE 147th Place. We checked one large Eastern Redcedar for Juniper Hairstreaks, finding none.

With Don Fraser, checking out the flowers and the butterflies for next Saturday's Goethe State Forest butterfly count. I forgot to record the weather at the start, but the weather at 1247 was sunny, 89 degrees ("feels like" 98), with S winds at 8 MPH. Forecast rain did not appear. Our itinerary for today was:

0845-0850: Wawa's along US-19 in Crystal River -- getting food and drink.

0921-1136: various spots along County Road 336 through Goethe State Forest (except for the powerlines just east of US 19) -- mostly checking on the status of the Marsh Rattlesnake Master (Eryngium aquaticum) plants. It seems as though some of the area was mowed in the past two months, as the plants were sparse and stunted, blooming when the plant was less than 12 inches tall. We saw no butterflies at all using the Eryngium. Skippers were scarce, and were mostly limited to Whirlabouts and Neamathla/Swarthy's skippers. Perhaps surprisingly, many Bristle Thistles were in full bloom, but almost all pollinators on them were bees; I did not see a single wasp all day! The ditches were all dried.

1139-1306: County Road 336 under the powerlines just east of US-19 -- Although scarce here too, the Marsh Rattlesnake Master approached its "normal" flowering height of 3-4 feet. The  beginning of the marsh on the south side of County Road 336 was dried. Don found a Byssus Skipper here.

1328-1338: the eastern side of SE 147th Place, but we did not enter Cedars of Lebanon Cemetery -- a trip to see if Tawny Emperors, Hackberry Emperors, or Goatweed Leafwings were around. (We saw both emperors but not the leafwing).

I treated Don to lunch at Applebee's in Crystal River.

It's very frustrating, so I suspect that I will never again use this Lumix. My cell phone (Samsung Galaxy A52) got heavy use today.

0837-1438: With Don Fraser and Wade Baker checking the blooming status of Bristle Thistle (well underway), blazing stars (Liatris; just getting started), Coastal Plain Honeycomb Head (not yet visible), and various other bug plants. I did not record the weather until 1343, when it was sunny, 92 degrees (‘feels like” 103), with light winds. We visited only three areas: the thistle pond on Rattlesnake Camp Road (0844-0935), various spots along 3 Bridge Road, including a small bit of the trail to Buford Spring, and one spot along Gopher Road (briefly). Afterward, we drove Gopher Road north to the gate at Hernando Hunt Club to show that area to Wade. We found two Juniper Hairstreaks at the second Red Cedar along Rattlesnake Camp Road, and a Dukes’ Skipper on Liatris on the northern half of 3 Bridge Road. I think I got a lifer Robber Fly or two, and a lifer beetle or two. One clump of goldenrod held a Jagged Ambush Bug eating a Cloudless Sulphur, a Green Lynx Spider eating a Jagged Ambush Bug (!), another Green Lynx Spider eating a Delta Scarab Beetle, and a third Green Lynx Spider eating something that it quickly dropped. We left the area at 1438 and I ate an early dinner at Hardee’s.

With Don Fraser and Wade Baker. The weather at the start was sunny, 84 degrees (“feels like” 95), and with WNW winds at 3 MPH. The weather at 1244 was sunny and 93 degrees (“feels like” 106);it was brutal out there today. We drove Rattlesnake Camp Road and visited the thistle pond (0913-1011) and made one other stop farther west (1027-1035). Then we drove the entirety of Scrub Island Road, but the shoulders had recently been mowed and we saw no flowers; we did not stop. We made several stops along 3 Bridge Road (1059-1423). Blazing stars and Coastal Plain Chaffhead are starting to bloom but are weeks away from their peak; we saw one Coastal Plain Honeycomb Head with a single flower. We found no flower moths (Schinia) despite constant searching. Bristle Thistles are in full bloom, and the (dried) pond along Rattlesnake Camp Road had dozens of swallowtails and Clouded Sulphurs and smaller number of skippers (just the usual species). I saw two “good” moths, a Kentucky Lichen Moth that Wade found, and two caterpillars of Pale-edged Selesia feeding on Sesbania. I found my first Eastern Redbud of the Area. We left around 1445.

My camera almost got thrown in the pond this morning, but I found a way to take some good photographs with it. But mostly, I used my cell phone, which died at 1333 because I forgot to bring my charger.

With Don Fraser and Chase Bonano; checking on the butterflies and moths. We stopped at several sites, as follows.

0908-0941 (I got a late start, the others had been there almost 30 minutes when I arrived): the thistle pond on Rattlesnake Road. FWC left the shoulders of the pond unmowed – maybe they followed my email to them? – so there are lots of Bristle Thistles in bloom, and lots of swallowtails and skippers (just regular stuff). I found a cluster of eggs here that iNaturalist says is from an Io Moth. I bought a brand new Panasonic Lumix FZ80D yesterday so I was eager to try it out on butterflies nectaring on thistles. It worked magically at first, then digressed quickly to taking unfocused photographs of blobs. I later learned that I needed to right-click the main button in back and then the camera focused beautifully. I have never had to that before (I think this is my 8th Lumix [but never an FZ80D before), so I have some tweaking to do. 

0951-0959: Rattlesnake Camp Road almost to 3 Bridge Road. Don spotted a Dukes’ Skipper (lifer for Chase) nectaring on blazing star, so we stopped for 10 minutes.

1015-1243: various stops in sandhills along 3 Bridge Road, whenever we saw blooming blazing star (Liatris). We searched for the Lynx Flower Moth that Alice Herden saw here this past week, but we did not find it. I found a “pug” caterpillar, the larva of the Southern Flannel Moth.

1252-1340: sandhills on the east side of North Road just north of Indigo Lane. There were many Coastalplain Honeycombhead (Balduina angustifolia) plants in full bloom, and we carefully searched every flower. We found six Fuller’s Flower Moths, possibly a record! We also found an Eastern Fence Lizard here. We left shortly afterward and exited the WEA about 1352.

All of my photographs were taken with a Samsung Galaxy A52 cell phone on the macro setting and using the built-in flashlight.
